fruit or grapefruit juice is ingested, the metabolizing enzyme is 
inhibited irreversibly, which reduces the normal metabolism of 
the drug. This reduction in metabolism allows more of the drug 
to reach the systemic circulation; the increase in blood levels of 
unmetabolized drug results in a greater pharmacologic effect 
and possible toxicity. Unfortunately, the effects of grapefruit on 
intestinal cytochrome P-450 3A4 last up to 72 hours. Therefore 
separating the ingestion of the grapefruit and the daily dose of 
drug does not appear to alleviate this interaction.
Competition between food and drugs such as propranolol 
(Inderal) and metoprolol (Lopressor) for metabolizing enzymes 
in the liver may alter the first-pass metabolism of these medica-
tions. The term first-pass refers to the hepatic inactivation of oral 
medications when they are given initially. Drugs absorbed from 
the intestinal tract by the portal circulation first are transported 
to the liver before they reach the systemic circulation. Because 
many drugs are metabolized during this first pass through the 
liver, only a small percentage of the original dose is actually avail-
able to the systemic circulation and the target organ. In some 
cases, however, this percentage can be increased by concurrent 
ingestion of food with the drug. When food and drug compete 
for the same metabolizing enzymes in the liver, more of the drug 
is likely to reach the systemic circulation, which can lead to a toxic 
effect if the dose titration occurs in a fasting state.
